agree.reason: The candid A1C data and the low-cost trial would make this wary reader take it seriously, but there is nothing to reassure someone who has quit three services: it never says the plan has no contract, that you can skip or cancel, or that you can swap meals or call the dietitian first.

honest.reason: It rightly drops the promise that the meals will lower A1C and states the limits of the 14-person sample, but it invents a reason customers stay ('they like the food') and ties the 0.6 average drop to the 10 improvers when the brief may mean the average across all 14.

works_the_facts.reason: Figures are repeated rather than worked: it never turns 37 of 88 into the roughly 42% of customers still there after six months, a strong point for a reader who quits within two months, and it never gives 10 of 14 as about 71%.

right_comparison.reason: The only alternative mentioned is losing $59 on the trial; the page never sets itself against what this reader has actually done, which is starting apps and services and quitting them, or against planning low-carb meals alone.

qualification.reason: Stating that the data is not a clinical study and that medication changes weren't tracked is honest and specific, but 'your results will depend on many things' gives the reader no checkpoint, date or number to judge it by.

objections.reason: The trial week answers 'will I like it', but the main fears of someone who has quit before (being locked in, getting bored of the food) go unanswered, even though no contract, skip or cancel any time, six swap choices and a 15-minute call with the dietitian were all available.

fit.reason: It is a sales page of about 400 words with a clear call to action, though it leaves out practical details such as the Thursday noon order cutoff, the 25-mile delivery area and the service's name.
